units: groups of different animals share the same bank without falling out
the birds with webbed feet search the mud with their beaks
these birds leave star-shaped marks pressed into the mud
rodents of a stocky build live in the belt of reeds
these rodents drive tunnels and eat the young stems
their soft fur keeps the wet off them
the insects hold to the dry part of the slope
the insects feed the animals that fly above
the bank reads as three levels stacked one upon another
text: Three sets of creatures hold the edge of the pond at once, and none of them gets in the way of another. Where the mud lies softest, the web-footed birds work their beaks through the silt, and the ground behind them keeps a scatter of star-shaped prints. A little higher, in among the flattened reeds, live the short thick-bodied rodents; they drive tunnels through the bank and strip the young stems down to the pith, and their downy coats turn the wet away. The dry face of the slope belongs to the insects, hardly noticed and past counting, and everything that flies above the water lives on them. Sit still long enough and the edge sorts itself into three floors stacked one on another: open water, then mud, then cropped grass. Each floor sets its own food, its own hours, its own quiet.

units: the writer holds that public argument has not kept pace with tracking methods
counting was first done by eye and written up on paper
coloured marks then made it possible to follow one particular animal
those marks unsettled the species least willing to be approached
small transmitters now record movement without a break
these devices also measure the depth of dives and the beat of the heart
the writer holds that each advance shifts the moral problem without settling it
a light device still alters what a bird spends in energy
the writer asks that an outside body approve every fitting of a device
text: Let me put it plainly: the watching of wild populations has changed out of all recognition, and the public argument has not kept pace. At the start a person stood on a bank and counted by eye, writing the totals up on paper afterwards. Coloured rings came next, and with them the power to follow one animal rather than a blur of them, though the shyest sorts were badly unsettled by the closeness such work asks for. Now a tag records movement without a break, and reads off the depth of a dive and the beat of a heart besides. Every step forward has shifted the moral problem along instead of settling it. A tag weighs almost nothing, yet it still alters what a bird spends in the air. My own view is firm: nothing should be fitted unless an outside panel has looked at the case and agreed to it.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who looks after the horses had not aimed at this work
an injury to the knee took her away from her first trade
this injury obliges her to move without haste
the fearful animals came close to her before the others did
she announces every movement by speaking before any touch
the unwilling animals turn biddable within a single season
neighbouring places send her the animals judged past helping
she puts her success down to a constraint of the body and not to a gift
she forbids the beginners in her charge to move at a run
text: The woman who has charge of the horses did not set out to do this work at all. An injury to the knee closed the trade she had trained for, and the stalls were what remained open to her. Because she limps, she moves without haste, and the timid animals, used to quick hands about them, were the first to come near her. Out of that enforced slowness a method grew. She learned to say aloud what she was about to do before her hand went anywhere, so that the most unwilling beasts turned biddable inside a season. Word spread, and neighbouring places began sending her the ones written off as past helping. She will not hear the word gift. The advantage, she says, was handed to her by her own body, and anyone willing to slow down would arrive at the same place. She now trains beginners, who are not allowed to run.

units: the reviewer finds the pictures of the film well made
the reviewer faults the telling for giving human motives to the animals
this lends the belief that survival follows from a considered choice
the viewer comes away moved but no better informed
the last part of the film does without any telling
these passages were shot at night with a heat camera
they follow a band of wolves crossing a wooded corridor
the want of speech makes this passage truer than the opening of the film
text: Nothing is wanting in the pictures: the framing holds, the patience shows, every surface comes through with real precision. It is the telling that lets the film down. Human motives are handed out freely, the she-wolf decides, the hawk chooses, the colony takes revenge, and the ease of it thins the whole thing, since survival begins to look like something weighed up and settled. One comes away moved and none the wiser. The cure was to hand, and the director found it in his closing part, where the night passages, taken with a heat camera, run almost without a word. A pack crosses a wooded corridor, halts, moves off again, and nothing is said over it. All at once the film is truer than anything before it. The lesson holds for the whole kind: film it and stop; explain it and betray it.

units: the writer writes to an acquaintance about two cats
the cat with striped fur was already hanging about behind the workshop
a second cat with ginger fur turned up not long ago
the striped cat hunts little and sleeps on the warmed metal sheet
the ginger cat is thin and eats greedily
the ginger cat keeps its distance from people
the writer tried feeding them in one place in two bowls
the ginger one ate what was in both bowls
the writer means to set the meals of the two animals apart
text: Do you remember that striped cat forever hanging about behind the workshop? He has a rival now, and the gap between the pair is worth a letter. The striped one hunts hardly at all, sleeps on the warm sheet of metal and waits to be waited on; a door creaks and he is already purring. The newcomer is ginger, thin, ravenous, and will not let you within three paces of him. One has worked out that people are a larder, the other that they are a threat. Where the first asks, the second helps himself. I tried feeding them at the same spot, in two bowls set well apart: a poor idea, since the ginger emptied both while the striped one stared at me as though I had sold him. So the meals will be pulled apart, one at first light and one after dark, and the pair left to it. Come and watch some evening.

units: a specialist in animal behaviour answers the questions of the reporter
the subject is the massed flights of birds above river mouths
the specialist puts forward three explanations
living in a crowd lowers the chance that any one bird is taken
the birds find food by watching those that come back well fed
the flock finds the fish in this way without a leader pointing them out
birds packed together hold their warmth better through the halts of the night
the specialist denies that any ranking exists in these flights
each bird sets its pace by the neighbours nearest to it
text: We put our questions to a specialist in animal behaviour about the massed flights of birds above the river mouths. Is there anything like an organisation behind them? Her answer comes in three parts. The first is safety: a bird that keeps company spreads the risk, and stands a smaller chance of being taken while it moves inside a shifting cloud. The second is news. Those coming home well fed are watched and followed, so the whole flock learns where the fish are lying without a leader pointing anything out. The third is warmth; pressed against one another through the halts of the night, the birds lose far less of it. Is there a ranking all the same? She will not have it. What she describes are local rules, each bird setting its pace by whoever is nearest, and a shape overhead that nobody willed.

units: the keeper of the herd comes to warn before the sun rises
he reports that one animal is missing
the neighbour holds that the mist makes the search useless
the keeper answers that the animal has been walking badly since the day before
three people set out together to look for the animal
the keeper explains that the beast follows smells instead of the herd
the neighbour catches the sound of breathing behind some scrub
the animal is found lying down and alive at the foot of the slope
the keeper carries the animal back on his shoulders
text: Before the sun was up the old keeper of the herd knocked at the shutter and said one of the beasts was missing. My neighbour, still in her shawl, told him nobody looks for a horned animal in mist and that the thing to do was wait. He answered that it had been walking badly since the day before and could not have gone far. The three of us went out. On the path he explained that the creature had a way of following smells instead of following its own kind. Then my neighbour stopped and said she could hear breathing, down below, behind the scrub. The keeper went over the edge, pushed the branches apart and called up that she was there, lying down but alive. He brought her up across his shoulders without a word of complaint. Walking home he said only that the next outing would be for her alone, and laughed quietly.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: taming reached first for the species that put up with human company
a species that lives in a crowd already knows an order of rank within it
such a species allows a stranger to take the leading place
a species that lives alone and holds ground refuses that place to a stranger
human groups kept the lines whose young would bear closeness
the animals hard to approach seldom bred within an enclosure
the sorting therefore went on without any settled plan
tamed animals show a shorter jaw and ears that hang down
these features come up together because they arise from the same cells of the embryo
text: Taming did not begin with the most useful creatures but with the most forbearing. A beast that lives in a crowd already stands somewhere in an order of rank, and will therefore let a stranger take the leading place, which one that lives alone and holds its own ground never grants. From that leaning a plain consequence follows: human groups held on only to the lines whose young could bear having people about them. The wary ones fled or struck out, and bred poorly behind a fence, so the sorting went on with almost nothing willed about it. Shape and temper then shifted together: the jaw grew shorter, the ears came down, the temper cooled, ripeness arrived later. Such features turn up as a set because they all trace back to the same cells in the embryo. Mildness was never taught. It was gathered in.

units: the frogs and their kin leave the woods for the ponds where they were born
their route crosses a road again and again
these animals with webbed feet go forward in small moves
they hold still in front of the beams of vehicles
they travel above all after the sun has gone down
a population of one place can die out within three seasons
a first measure is a low fence that leads the animals towards a tunnel
this work costs a great deal but asks for no watching over
a second measure closes the road on the nights of heaviest movement
both measures suppose that the usual routes have been found beforehand
text: When the mild season comes round, frogs and their kin leave the woods for the ponds they hatched in. The way there crosses a road more often than not, and the losses run high: these web-footed travellers advance in short hops, freeze in the beams of oncoming traffic, and set off mostly once the sun is down, at the hour when driving is still fast. A population can be wiped from a place in three seasons. Two answers have been tried. The first lays a low fence along the verge, steering the animals towards a pipe that runs beneath the surfacing; the work costs dearly but needs nobody to mind it. The second, much lighter, shuts the road on the nights of heaviest movement. Both call for the old crossing places to have been traced first, which nothing but patient watching will give you.

units: two young dogs of the same age reached the shelter on the same evening
the first dog is heavily built and carries grey patches
the first dog lets itself be touched and looks for company
the second dog takes fright at noises and comes out only once night has fallen
the staff thought the first dog would be taken very quickly
it was the second dog that left the shelter first
a household kept it precisely because it held back
this household judged its home too quiet for a restless animal
the first dog waited until the autumn
the man in charge concludes that the fondest animal is not the first to be taken
text: Nobody would have put money on the pup that kept to the back of its kennel. Two dogs of the same age had been left at the shelter on the same evening, and the staff never tired of setting one against the other. The first, heavy and flecked with grey, took handling without a murmur; she ate anything, slept anywhere, and pushed her head forward for a stroke the moment a door moved. The second flinched at the knock of a bucket and left her shelter only after dark. A week would see the first one rehomed, the keepers said. It was the second that found a household first. She was chosen for the very hiding that had counted against her, by people who said their rooms were too still to suit a restless animal. The flecked one waited until autumn. The most winning animal, says the man in charge, is never the first to go.
